meta.subject: US_HISTORY
meta.author: bank-team-us-history
meta.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: What did declaring independence primarily accomplish?

options.text: It asserted self-government and broke imperial ties
It ended all foreign trade immediately
It created a monarchy at home

questions.explanation: Independence asserted self-government. The tempting trade answer confuses sovereignty with economics.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a weakness of the Articles
questions.stem: What was a key weakness of the Articles of Confederation?

options.text: They gave Congress too much taxing power
They left Congress without reliable revenue

options.misconception: attributes later features to the Articles

questions.explanation: Congress lacked reliable revenue. The tempting too-much-power answer reverses the weakness.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why the Convention was called
questions.stem: Why was the Constitutional Convention called?

answer.exemplar: The Constitutional Convention was called because the Articles proved too weak to manage debt, trade, and disorder, prompting leaders to seek a stronger federal framework.

questions.explanation: The Articles proved too weak. The tempting single-issue answer ignores the broader crisis.

questions.stem: What does federalism mean in this context?

options.text: All power rests in the capital
States have no power at all
Power is divided between national and state governments

questions.explanation: Federalism divides power. The tempting all-power-in-capital answer describes unitary rule.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose of the Bill of Rights
questions.stem: What did the Bill of Rights primarily secure?
questions.explanation: The Bill secured liberties. The tempting unlimited-power answer reverses its purpose.

questions.stem: What did the Constitution establish?

options.text: A loose alliance with no centre
options.misconception: describes the Articles, not the Constitution

options.text: Direct rule by a single king
A stronger federal government with separated powers

questions.explanation: The Constitution created a stronger federal government. The tempting loose-alliance answer describes the Articles.

stimulus.body: Federalists argued a strong union was needed, while Anti-Federalists warned that distant power threatened liberty and demanded a bill of rights.

questions.stem: What was the core of the ratification debate?

options.text: Whether to keep the Articles unchanged
Balancing stronger union with protected liberty

questions.explanation: The debate balanced union and liberty. The tempting keep-Articles answer ignores the new proposal.

questions.stem: What characterised the early republic?

options.text: Immediate national unity on all issues

questions.explanation: The early republic experimented with institutions. The tempting unity answer overstates cohesion.

questions.stem: How does the Constitution differ from the Declaration?

options.text: The Declaration announces principles; the Constitution structures government

questions.explanation: The Declaration states principles, the Constitution structures government. The tempting identical answer collapses them.

stimulus.body: A speaker claims independence alone solved all colonial grievances, including taxation and representation.

questions.stem: Is this claim accurate?

options.text: No, because independence created new challenges

questions.explanation: Independence created new challenges. The tempting yes answer treats sovereignty as a cure-all.

questions.learningObjective: Apply Articles weakness to a case
questions.stem: Under the Articles, why could Congress not pay war debts?

options.text: Because it lacked taxing power and relied on states

questions.explanation: Congress relied on state contributions. The tempting free-taxation answer reverses the limit.

stimulus.body: Critics say the Convention exceeded its mandate by drafting a new constitution instead of revising the Articles.

questions.stem: How should this criticism be assessed?

options.text: It is irrelevant, since results justify means
It proves the Convention was illegal
It has merit, but the new frame was ratified

questions.explanation: The criticism has merit but ratification followed. The tempting results-justify-means answer ignores process.

questions.stem: In a federal system, who handles a local school curriculum?

options.text: No one, since it is unregulated
Primarily the state or local government

questions.explanation: Local curricula are state or local matters. The tempting national-only answer centralises wrongly.

questions.stem: Why did Anti-Federalists insist on a Bill of Rights?

answer.exemplar: Anti-Federalists insisted on a Bill of Rights because they feared a strong central government could infringe liberties unless explicit protections were written into the Constitution.

questions.explanation: They feared infringement of liberties. The tempting unnecessary answer ignores their concerns.

stimulus.body: A commentator claims the Constitution created a perfect balance of power that never needed amendment.

questions.stem: Is this claim accurate?

options.text: No, because amendments followed soon after
Yes, because the design was flawless

questions.explanation: Amendments followed, showing imperfection. The tempting flawless answer ignores the Bill of Rights.

questions.stem: What was the overall outcome of the ratification debate?

answer.exemplar: The ratification debate ended in adoption of the Constitution with a promise of amendments, blending Federalist union with Anti-Federalist liberty protections.

questions.explanation: The Constitution was adopted with promised amendments. The tempting pure-Federalist answer ignores concessions.

questions.stem: Was the early republic stable?

options.text: Stable in framework but contested in practice

questions.explanation: The framework held despite contestation. The tempting perfect-stability answer overstates early calm.

questions.learningObjective: Apply document purpose to a case
questions.stem: Which document would you cite to argue that government needs consent?
questions.explanation: The Declaration states consent of the governed. The tempting Constitution answer confuses structure with principle.

questions.stem: What did independence not immediately change?

answer.exemplar: Independence did not immediately change economic dependence, social hierarchies, or the practical challenges of governing a diverse and war-torn population.

questions.explanation: Independence left economic and social structures intact. The tempting everything-changed answer overstates its reach.

questions.stem: What legacy did the Articles leave?

answer.exemplar: The Articles left a legacy of state sovereignty and a demonstration that a weak centre could not manage national problems, shaping the stronger Constitution.

questions.explanation: The Articles showed weakness of a loose centre. The tempting no-legacy answer ignores their influence.

questions.stem: What was the Great Compromise?

options.text: Bicameral legislature with population and equal state representation

options.misconception: describes the Virginia Plan, not the compromise

questions.explanation: The Great Compromise created a bicameral legislature. The tempting single-chamber answer describes a rejected plan.

stimulus.body: A critic argues federalism always favours the national government and leaves states powerless.

questions.stem: Is this criticism accurate?

options.text: Yes, because states have no powers
No, because states retain significant powers
No, because the national government is powerless

questions.explanation: States retain significant powers. The tempting national-dominance answer overstates centralisation.

questions.stem: Which amendment protects against unreasonable searches?
questions.explanation: The Fourth Amendment protects against unreasonable searches. The tempting First Amendment answer confuses liberties.

questions.stem: How does the Constitution allow for change?

answer.exemplar: The Constitution allows change through amendments and interpretation, letting it adapt to new circumstances without being rewritten from scratch.

questions.explanation: Amendments and interpretation allow adaptation. The tempting rigidity answer ignores these mechanisms.

questions.stem: Why did some states demand amendments before ratifying?

options.text: To protect liberties against new federal power

questions.explanation: States sought liberty protections. The tempting opposition-to-all-government answer misreads their caution.

questions.stem: What challenges defined the early republic?

answer.exemplar: The early republic faced challenges of building institutions, managing debt, defining federal-state relations, and navigating foreign threats while maintaining unity.

questions.explanation: Institutions, debt, federalism, and foreign threats all challenged the early republic. The tempting single-challenge answer narrows too much.

stimulus.body: A writer claims the Declaration of Independence created the federal government and its institutions.

questions.stem: Is this claim accurate?

options.text: No, because it announced principles, not institutions
No, because it was never adopted

questions.explanation: The Declaration announced principles, not institutions. The tempting nationhood answer confuses declaration with constitution.

questions.stem: If a colony declares independence, what must it then do?

options.misconception: ignores the need to build government

questions.explanation: Independence requires building institutions. The tempting nothing-further answer ignores governance.

questions.stem: Why were the Articles designed to be weak?

answer.exemplar: The Articles were designed to be weak because recent experience with British central power made leaders wary of a strong national government, so they favoured state sovereignty.

questions.explanation: Leaders feared central power after British rule. The tempting accident answer ignores deliberate design.

questions.stem: What was the Convention's broader significance?

answer.exemplar: The Convention's broader significance was replacing a failing confederation with a durable federal republic, setting a precedent for constitutional government.

questions.explanation: It replaced a failing confederation. The tempting minor-revision answer understates the change.

questions.stem: What tension does federalism create?

options.text: Between national authority and state autonomy

questions.explanation: Federalism tensions national authority against state autonomy. The tempting no-tension answer denies reality.

stimulus.body: A historian argues the Bill of Rights was unnecessary because the Constitution already limited government power sufficiently.

questions.stem: How should this argument be assessed?

options.text: It is overstated, since explicit protections mattered

questions.explanation: Explicit protections mattered. The tempting fully-correct answer ignores Anti-Federalist pressure.

questions.stem: Which principle prevents any one branch from dominating?
questions.explanation: Checks and balances prevent dominance. The tempting hereditary answer confuses republic with monarchy.

questions.stem: What did Federalists argue during ratification?

answer.exemplar: Federalists argued that a stronger union was essential for security, commerce, and stability, and that the Constitution's structure would prevent tyranny.

questions.explanation: Federalists stressed union and structure. The tempting Anti-Federalist view misattributes their argument.

stimulus.body: A leader claims the early republic's financial plan was universally accepted and caused no controversy.

questions.stem: Is this claim accurate?

options.text: No, because financial plans sparked fierce debate
Yes, because no one opposed Hamilton
No, because the plan was rejected

questions.explanation: Financial plans sparked debate. The tempting unity answer overstates consensus.

questions.stem: How do the founding documents work together?

answer.exemplar: The founding documents work together by stating principles, creating institutions, and protecting rights, each addressing a different need of self-government.

questions.explanation: They address different needs. The tempting redundant answer ignores their distinct roles.

stimulus.body: A speech declares independence a clean break with no continuities, ignoring shared legal traditions and economic ties.

questions.stem: Is this portrayal accurate?
questions.explanation: Continuities persisted. The tempting total-break answer overstates the rupture.

questions.stem: Under the Articles, how could a state ignore a national request?

options.text: It could not, since requests were binding
It had to obey foreign powers instead
It could refuse, since compliance was voluntary

questions.explanation: Compliance was voluntary. The tempting binding answer overstates national authority.

questions.stem: What issue did the Three-Fifths Compromise address?

options.text: Counting enslaved people for representation and taxation

questions.explanation: It counted enslaved people for representation and taxation. The tempting exports answer confuses issues.

questions.stem: Why was federalism chosen over a unitary system?

answer.exemplar: Federalism was chosen to balance effective national governance with protection of state autonomy, avoiding both the weakness of the Articles and the tyranny of centralised rule.

questions.explanation: It balanced national and state power. The tempting unitary answer ignores the fear of centralisation.

questions.stem: What does the First Amendment protect?

options.text: Only the right to bear arms
Speech, religion, press, assembly, and petition

questions.explanation: The First Amendment protects speech, religion, press, assembly, and petition. The tempting arms answer confuses amendments.

stimulus.body: A state passes a law conflicting with the federal Constitution, claiming state sovereignty overrides federal law.

questions.stem: Is the state's claim valid?

options.text: No, because states have no laws
Yes, because the Constitution is advisory
No, because federal law is supreme

questions.explanation: Federal law is supreme. The tempting state-sovereignty answer overstates state power.

questions.stem: Which group supported ratification most strongly?
questions.explanation: Federalists supported ratification. The tempting Anti-Federalists answer reverses the groups.

questions.stem: What foreign policy challenge faced the early republic?

answer.exemplar: The early republic faced the challenge of navigating great-power rivalries without being drawn into war, while maintaining neutrality and trade.

questions.explanation: Great-power rivalries threatened neutrality. The tempting isolation answer ignores the difficulty of neutrality.

stimulus.body: A claim states the Constitution directly copied British parliamentary structure without alteration.

questions.stem: Is this claim accurate?

options.text: Yes, because no changes were made
No, because the Constitution innovated separated powers
No, because it copied France instead

questions.explanation: The Constitution innovated with separated powers. The tempting identical answer overstates similarity to Britain.

questions.stem: What does independence mean beyond separation?

answer.exemplar: Independence means not only separating from empire but also assuming responsibility for self-government, defence, and the rights of the governed.

questions.explanation: Independence includes responsibility for self-government. The tempting separation-only answer narrows its meaning.

questions.stem: Were the Articles entirely ineffective?

options.text: Yes, because they were never used
No, they managed some wartime and diplomatic tasks

questions.explanation: The Articles managed some wartime and diplomatic tasks. The tempting nothing answer understates them.

questions.stem: Which plan proposed representation by population?
questions.explanation: The Virginia Plan proposed population-based representation. The tempting New Jersey answer confuses plans.

questions.stem: Which level of government ratifies constitutional amendments?

options.text: The states through their legislatures or conventions
No one, since amendments are automatic

questions.explanation: States ratify amendments. The tempting president answer confuses executive with ratification.

questions.stem: Why were the first ten amendments added?

answer.exemplar: The first ten amendments were added to secure individual liberties and limit federal power, addressing Anti-Federalist demands and reassuring ratifiers.

questions.explanation: They secured liberties and limited federal power. The tempting unnecessary answer ignores ratification politics.

questions.stem: What does separation of powers achieve?

options.text: Prevention of tyranny by dividing government

questions.explanation: Separation prevents tyranny. The tempting concentration answer reverses the purpose.

stimulus.body: An Anti-Federalist warns that a standing army under the new Constitution will destroy liberty, citing European examples.

questions.stem: How should this warning be assessed?

options.text: It reflects a genuine fear, though the Constitution also provides civilian control
It is baseless, since armies are harmless
It shows Anti-Federalists wanted no defence

questions.explanation: The fear was genuine but civilian control exists. The tempting baseless answer denies the concern's merit.

questions.stem: Which early republic development strengthened federal power?
questions.explanation: Suppressing the Whiskey Rebellion strengthened federal power. The tempting abolition answer reverses policy.

questions.stem: What limitation did the founding documents share regarding slavery?

answer.exemplar: The founding documents largely avoided or compromised on slavery, leaving the institution intact and creating tensions that later erupted.

questions.explanation: They avoided or compromised on slavery. The tempting resolved answer ignores the unresolved issue.

stimulus.body: A commentator claims American independence immediately inspired all colonies worldwide to revolt successfully.

questions.stem: Is this claim accurate?

options.text: No, because independence had no influence
Yes, because all colonies revolted at once
No, because inspiration took time and context

questions.explanation: Inspiration took time and context. The tempting instant answer overstates the speed.

questions.stem: What lesson did the Articles teach?

answer.exemplar: The Articles taught that a government lacking taxing and coercive power cannot sustain itself, prompting a stronger federal design.

questions.explanation: Weakness taught the need for stronger power. The tempting no-lesson answer ignores their influence.

questions.stem: Why did the Convention meet in secret?

options.text: To allow free debate without public pressure

questions.explanation: Secrecy allowed free debate. The tempting corruption answer assumes bad faith.

stimulus.body: A writer claims federalism has remained unchanged since 1787, with no shift in national-state balance.

questions.stem: Is this claim accurate?

options.text: Yes, because the text is fixed
No, because practice has shifted toward national power

questions.explanation: Practice shifted toward national power. The tempting fixed-text answer confuses text with practice.

questions.stem: Which amendment guarantees a speedy trial?
questions.explanation: The Sixth Amendment guarantees a speedy trial. The tempting First Amendment answer confuses liberties.

questions.stem: What lasting influence did the founding documents have?

answer.exemplar: The founding documents had lasting influence by providing a framework for self-government, rights, and constitutional change that shaped later democratic movements.

questions.explanation: They provided a framework shaping later movements. The tempting no-influence answer understates their reach.
